What small business website design means here

Small business website design at Dominion Web Design Pro is simple to describe. Maurice Johnson looks at your business, writes every page in plain words for your customers, builds the site so it works on a phone, and connects it to your domain and your contact form. You see a demo before any money changes hands.

That is a narrower job than some web companies sell, and it is on purpose. A barber, an insurance office, a landscaper or a bakery does not need a software project. It needs a website that answers the questions a stranger asks before calling: what do you do, where, when are you open, and how do I reach you.

Many owners looking for a small business website already have something online. A free builder site they started on a Sunday and never finished. A page an old vendor still controls. A Facebook profile doing the work of a website. Any of those can be the starting point.

The pages a small business website needs

Here is the page plan we start from. Not every business needs all of it, and some need more, but if a site is missing one of the first five, customers notice the gap before you do.

PageWhat it is forWhat belongs on it
HomeTells a visitor in five seconds whether they are in the right placeWhat you do, the towns you serve, one clear way to call or message, and a short reason to pick you
ServicesLets people check that you do the exact job they needEach service named the way customers say it, with a short honest description
AboutAnswers "who am I dealing with?"Who owns the business, how long you have been at it if you want to say, and how you work
ContactTurns a reader into a phone call or a messagePhone, form, hours, address or service radius, and a map
Service areaShows which towns you coverThe towns and neighborhoods you actually drive to or ship to
GalleryProof you can seeYour own photos of real work, storefront or products
Separate service pagesOne page per main job people search for by nameDetails, common questions and what the job involves
City pagesReach people searching in towns beyond your home baseWriting about that town and how you serve it, researched first

The first five rows are the Starter package. The Pro package adds the gallery, five more pages and ten city pages. The Agency package starts with keyword research and builds a page for each town-and-service pair the research says people search for.

Three ways a small business website can be laid out

People ask for small business website examples so they can picture their own. These are structure patterns, not client sites: three common kinds of local business and the shape of the website that fits each one.

The service business that drives to you

A plumber, pest control company or mobile detailer. Customers never visit the shop, so the address matters less than the service radius. The home page leads with the phone number and the towns covered. Each main service gets its own page because people search "water heater repair" and "drain cleaning" separately.

The shop customers walk into

A boutique, a cafe, a salon or a hardware store. Hours, parking and the map go near the top. Photos of the inside of the place do more than any paragraph. The services page may be a menu, a price list or a short list of brands carried.

The office people book

An accountant, insurance agent, counselor or tutor. Trust carries the sale, so the about page gets real attention: who you are, what you will and will not take on, and what the first appointment looks like. The contact page explains how to book and what to bring.

Common problems we see on small business websites

Most small business sites do not fail for lack of design. They fail on a handful of plain things that cost calls every week.

  • The phone number is hard to tap. On a phone, the number should be a button near the top of every page, not an image of a number and not hidden in the footer.
  • Nobody can tell where you work. A site that never names its towns leaves search engines and customers guessing.
  • One page tries to say everything. A single long page with every service on it is hard to read and hard for search to match to a specific job.
  • Words written for the owner, not the customer. Mission statements and industry terms read like filler. Customers want to know whether you do their job, when you can come and roughly what happens next.
  • The owner cannot get in. The domain, the hosting or the login belongs to a vendor who stopped answering. That is the most expensive problem on the list, and it is avoidable.
  • The form goes nowhere. A contact form that sends messages to an old inbox looks fine and quietly loses every lead.

How we build it: demo first, hand-written pages

The process starts with the free demo. You give a business name and trade, a preview site is built, and you look at it on your own phone. Nothing is owed for that. If you like where it is going, you choose a package; if not, you walk away.

After you choose, Maurice writes each page himself. He reads what you already have online, asks what you do and do not want to take on, and writes in the words your customers use when they search. Nothing is pulled from a library of stock paragraphs. That is slower, and it is the part most low-cost website development skips.

Then come the plain technical jobs that a small business website setup needs: the site works on phones, tablets and desktops; the contact form emails every lead to you; every page gets a title and description; the sitemap is submitted to Google; Google Maps and your hours go on the page; and the Facebook and Instagram links are connected. Web design for startups and brand new businesses

A startup has a particular problem: no reviews yet, no gallery of past work, maybe not even a sign on the door. The temptation is to fill the gap with stock photos of smiling strangers and a few borrowed quotes. Do not do it. Customers can tell, and fake reviews create trouble you do not need.

What a new business site should do instead is be specific. Name the services. Name the towns. Say who you are and why you started. Put up your own photos, even phone photos of your truck, your tools or your counter. Add the reviews and the gallery as they come in.

Before any of that, register the domain in the business's own name. The U.S. Small Business Administration says that if you want an online presence, start by registering a domain name, and it advises buying web design, hosting and domain names in the company's name rather than the owner's. That is good advice for an established shop too.

Which package fits your small business

A useful rule: pick the package that matches how far your customers come from. If they are mostly in one town, Starter covers it. If you work across several towns and want a page that speaks to each one, Pro's ten city pages are built for that. If you serve a whole region with several distinct services, Agency starts with the research and writes a page for each combination worth having.

When a different option makes more sense

Honest answer: not every small business needs us. If you sell a large catalog of products online, you want a store platform built for checkout and inventory, which is not what these packages build. If you enjoy tinkering and have more time than budget, a do-it-yourself builder can work, and the builder versus web designer guide lays out that choice fairly. If you need a large custom web application, hire a development firm.

Where we fit is the local business that wants a clear, honest website with real words on it, owned outright, built by someone who will answer for it.

The quickest way to judge whether a small business website from here fits your shop is to see one. Ask for the free demo and look at it on your phone tonight.

Common questions

What pages does a small business website need?

Five covers most local businesses: a home page, a services page, an about page, a contact page and a service area page. That is exactly what the Starter package builds. Add separate pages for each main service, a photo gallery and city pages when customers search for those things separately, which is where the Pro and Agency packages come in.

How much does small business website design cost?

Here it is $497 for Starter, $997 for Pro or $1,997 for Agency, each paid once. Hosting, maintenance and updates are included while you keep the AI agent, or $49 a month without it. Elsewhere the range is wide; the small business website cost guide walks through what other options charge and why.

Do I need a website if my business already has a Facebook page?

Facebook is useful, but you do not own it, it does not show your services the way a search engine reads them, and plenty of customers never log in. A website is the address you control. Keep the Facebook page and link the two together; the Starter package puts those links on the site.

Can a brand new startup get a website before it has customers or reviews?

Yes, and that is a good time to do it. A startup site does not need reviews or a portfolio to be useful. It needs to say plainly what you do, where you do it and how to reach you. We will not invent reviews or past jobs to make a new business look older, and you should not let anyone else do that either.

Is there a small business website designer near me?

Maurice Johnson works from Big Sandy in East Texas and builds sites for small businesses anywhere in the United States. You see the demo by link, talk by phone and approve pages by email. If you are near Tyler, Longview or Gilmer you are close to home; if you are not, the work goes just as smoothly at a distance.

How long does it take to build a small business website?

A Starter site goes live in 7 to 14 days. Agency sites arrive in waves, with the first pages live inside two weeks. The biggest delay is usually waiting on photos, hours and service details, so gather those early.
